exhibit.title: Representative SW1# show etherchannel summary
exhibit.text:
Group  Port-channel  Protocol  Ports
1      Po1(SU)       LACP      Fa0/23(P) Fa0/24(P)

prompt: Which statement does the summary support?
options: Po1 is routed and both members are passive.
Po1 is Layer 2 and in use; both listed members are bundled.
Po1 carries every VLAN on the switch.
One flow can necessarily use the sum of both member speeds.
explanation: S means Layer 2, U means in use and P on a member means bundled. The summary shows formation, not VLAN service or single-flow speed.

whyWrong.0: R means routed, and P means bundled, not passive.
whyWrong.2: Which VLANs are carried needs a separate trunk check.
whyWrong.3: Hashing sends a given flow over one member.

prompt: Which two mode pairs can form an LACP bundle? (Choose two.)
options: active / active
passive / passive
desirable / auto
active / passive
explanation: At least one LACP end must be active. Active/active and active/passive both form a bundle.

whyWrong.1: Neither passive end initiates, so passive/passive never forms.

prompt: How does STP treat a Layer 2 EtherChannel?
options: As one logical STP interface that can still be blocked when required.
As separate competing STP ports for every active member.
As an instruction to disable STP for the entire VLAN.
As a routed interface that never carries Layer 2 frames.
explanation: STP sees the port channel as one logical port. That logical port can still be blocked when STP needs it to be.

whyWrong.1: STP sees the bundle, not each member.
whyWrong.2: EtherChannel does not turn STP off.
whyWrong.3: A Layer 2 EtherChannel still carries Layer 2 frames.

exhibit.title: Representative D1# show etherchannel summary
exhibit.text:
Group  Port-channel  Protocol  Ports
1      Po1(RU)       LACP      Fa0/1(P) Fa0/2(P)

prompt: What does RU mean in this summary?
options: Layer 2 and in use.
Layer 3 and down.
Layer 2 and suspended.
Layer 3 and in use.
explanation: R means Layer 3 and U means in use. P on the members means both joined the bundle.

whyWrong.0: Layer 2 is S, and this summary shows R.
whyWrong.1: U means in use, not down.
whyWrong.2: The logical flags are R and U, and a member s flag means suspended.

prompt: Which two settings must match across members of a Layer 2 EtherChannel? (Choose two.)
options: Every local group number must equal the group number at the far end.
Member speed and duplex.
Member trunk/access mode and relevant VLAN settings.
Every member must have a different IPv4 subnet.
explanation: Members need the same speed and duplex, and the same trunk or access mode and VLAN settings. Group numbers are local and need not match.

whyWrong.0: Group numbers are locally significant and need not match the far end.
whyWrong.3: Layer 2 members have no IP address of their own.

prompt: Which statement correctly compares PAgP and LACP?
options: PAgP uses desirable and auto; LACP uses active and passive.
PAgP uses active and passive; LACP uses desirable and auto.
PAgP auto and LACP passive negotiate directly with each other.
Static on is the initiating mode of both protocols.
explanation: PAgP is Cisco's protocol and uses desirable and auto. LACP is the standard protocol and uses active and passive.

whyWrong.2: PAgP and LACP are different protocols and cannot negotiate together.
whyWrong.3: on is static and negotiates nothing.

prompt: Which command on a supporting IOS image displays the LACP partner information learned for bundle members?
options: show lacp neighbor
show ip route
show interfaces trunk
show vlan brief
explanation: show lacp neighbor lists the LACP partner for each member, including system and port IDs. Compare partner identity across members.

whyWrong.1: The routing table has no LACP partner information.
whyWrong.2: Trunk output shows VLANs, not LACP partners.
whyWrong.3: The VLAN database has no LACP information.

prompt: What does passive mean once an LACP bundle has formed?
options: It keeps all its members as backup-only data links.
It responds to negotiation; its bundled members can still forward data.
It switches the bundle to PAgP after the active peer is found.
It transmits data only if the active endpoint's links fail.
explanation: Active and passive describe who starts LACP negotiation, not which links carry data. Once formed, all bundled members forward traffic from both ends.

whyWrong.0: Passive does not make members backup-only.
whyWrong.3: Passive members forward data normally, not only after a failure.

prompt: All intended LACP members on both switches are passive. Links and VLAN settings are correct, but the bundle does not form. What fixes it?
options: Change only the remote channel-group number to match the local number.
Change both trunk native VLANs from 99 to 1.
Configure the intended members on at least one endpoint as LACP active.
Change one endpoint to mode on while leaving the other passive.
explanation: Passive/passive has no initiator. Set the members on at least one switch to active.

whyWrong.0: Group numbers are local and need not match.
whyWrong.1: Native VLANs are already compatible and do not start LACP.
whyWrong.3: on does not negotiate LACP, so it cannot pair with passive.

prompt: Four 1-Gbps links form a healthy EtherChannel. The hash puts one large TCP flow on one member. What is that flow's maximum speed?
options: 1 Gbps
2 Gbps
4 Gbps
8 Gbps
explanation: A single flow uses a single member, so it is limited to 1 Gbps. The 4 Gbps is aggregate capacity across many flows.

whyWrong.1: The hash does not split the flow across two members.
whyWrong.2: 4 Gbps is the total across all members, not one flow.
whyWrong.3: Counting both directions does not speed up one flow.

prompt: Which plan creates a routed EtherChannel between two multilayer switches?
options: Give every member the same IPv4 address and leave the port channel unnumbered.
Configure Po1 as an 802.1Q trunk and put the peer-link address on each member.
Assign a different subnet to every member; LACP combines the routes.
Create routed, addressed Po1 first; then add unnumbered routed members.
explanation: Create the routed port channel and give it the IP address. Then add members as routed ports with no IP address.

whyWrong.0: Members do not carry the port channel's address.
whyWrong.1: A Layer 2 trunk with addressed members is not a routed bundle.
whyWrong.2: LACP bundles links and does not combine routed subnets.

exhibit.title: Representative failure evidence
exhibit.text:
Po1(SU) LACP Fa0/23(P) Fa0/24(s)
Recorded log reason: vlan mask is different

prompt: The configuration shows Po1 and Fa0/23 allow VLANs 10,99 but Fa0/24 allows 10,20,99, and the log reports a VLAN mask mismatch. What do you check first?
options: The trunk allowed list only at the remote end.
Local trunk-setting consistency between Po1 and both physical members.
Whether the local and remote channel-group numbers are identical.
Whether passive mode is forbidden as an LACP response mode.
explanation: Members must match the port channel's trunk settings. Fa0/24 has a different allowed list, so fix the local settings first.

whyWrong.0: The log and local configuration point to the local member first.
whyWrong.2: Group numbers are local and need not match.
whyWrong.3: Passive is a valid LACP mode.

prompt: A virtualized server needs a two-link LACP connection to a switch. What must you confirm first?
options: The server has two NICs, which guarantees LACP support.
Each NIC reaches a different independent switch; that always creates one LACP partner.
The endpoint supports and uses LACP with compatible VLAN and partner configuration.
The host uses any teaming mode, because all teaming modes exchange LACP.
explanation: The server must support LACP and be set to use it, with compatible VLANs. Other teaming modes do not speak LACP.

whyWrong.0: Two NICs do not guarantee LACP support.
whyWrong.1: Links to separate independent switches do not form one LACP partner.
whyWrong.3: Only the LACP teaming mode exchanges LACP.

prompt: SW1 members use mode on and SW2 members use mode active. Cables and VLANs match. What happens?
options: They form LACP after both sides choose the same group number.
SW1’s on mode cannot provide the LACP negotiation expected by SW2; use a compatible mode pair.
The pairing is identical to active/passive.
Both sides are guaranteed to continue forwarding safely through independent links.
explanation: on is static and sends no LACP, while active expects LACP replies. The pair does not form a proper bundle, so use a matching pair such as active/active.

whyWrong.0: Group numbers do not make a static port speak LACP.
whyWrong.2: on is static, and passive is an LACP mode.
whyWrong.3: A mismatched bundle can cause loss or loops.

exhibit.title: Recorded device and traffic observations
exhibit.text:
Configured hash method: src-mac
Most transmitted frames: source MAC 0011.2233.4455
Both members: bundled (P)

prompt: A port channel hashes on source MAC, and most frames share one source MAC, the upstream router's. Why does one member carry most of the traffic?
options: The switch assigns each successive frame to the next member.
LACP requires the active side to use only one member.
The native VLAN automatically chooses the first member.
The repeated source-MAC hash input can repeatedly select the same member.
explanation: The hash is deterministic. The same source MAC always produces the same member.

whyWrong.0: The switch hashes and does not rotate members per frame.
whyWrong.2: The native VLAN does not pick a member.

prompt: SW1 uses channel-group 1 and SW2 uses channel-group 5. Both are active, member settings match and both links reach the same partner. What happens?
options: The mismatch prevents LACP negotiation.
The group numbers must be changed before any traffic can pass.
The bundle can form; the numbers identify the local port channels.
Only the link with the lower physical interface number can join.
explanation: Channel-group numbers are local to each switch. The bundle forms even with different numbers.

whyWrong.0: LACP does not need matching group numbers.
whyWrong.3: Group numbers do not choose a single member.

prompt: One 1-Gbps member of a four-member bundle fails and three stay bundled. One stable flow uses one member. Which two statements are correct? (Choose two.)
options: Aggregate capacity remains 4 Gbps per direction.
Aggregate capacity is up to 3 Gbps per direction.
The selected flow's member-link ceiling becomes 3 Gbps.
The selected flow's member-link ceiling remains 1 Gbps.
The two full-duplex directions give that one flow 6 Gbps.
explanation: Three members give up to 3 Gbps aggregate per direction. The one flow still uses one member and is limited to 1 Gbps.

whyWrong.0: The failed member no longer adds capacity.
whyWrong.2: One flow uses one member, so 1 Gbps is its maximum.
whyWrong.4: Counting both directions does not speed up one flow.

exhibit.title: Supplied acceptance checks
exhibit.text:
Both switches: Po1(SU), LACP, both intended members P
Both VLAN databases: VLANs 10,20,99 active
Both endpoint pairs: correct access VLANs and same-subnet IP settings
SW1 Po1: native 99, allowed/active/forwarding 10,20,99
SW2 Po1: native 99, allowed/active/forwarding 10,99

prompt: VLAN 10 clients work but the VLAN 20 pair does not. Which fix follows?
options: Re-create Po1 with static on at both ends.
Set VLAN 20 as native on both port channels.
Allow VLAN 20 on SW2 Po1; check its members.
Move the VLAN 20 clients into VLAN 10.
explanation: The bundle is up, but SW2's Po1 trunk does not allow VLAN 20. Add VLAN 20 to its allowed list and check the members.

whyWrong.0: LACP is working, so re-creating it is not the fix.
whyWrong.1: The native VLAN agrees and has nothing to do with the omitted VLAN.
whyWrong.3: Moving the clients breaks the VLAN design.

exhibit.title: Supplied routed-bundle acceptance evidence
exhibit.text:
Plan: D1 10.13.12.1/30, D2 10.13.12.2/30
D1: Po1(RU), both members P; Po1 IP 10.13.12.1/30
D2: Po1(RU), both members P; Po1 IP 10.13.12.6/30
Physical members are routed and unnumbered; no traffic filters

prompt: LACP is up but the directly connected peer ping fails. Which change matches the approved /30 plan?
options: Set D1's physical members to 10.13.12.1/30.
Set D2 Port-channel1 to 10.13.12.2/30.
Put 10.13.12.6/30 on D1 as a second member address.
Set both Port-channel1 interfaces to 10.13.12.1/30.
explanation: 10.13.12.1/30 is in 10.13.12.0/30, whose usable addresses are .1 and .2. D2's Port-channel1 must be .2, not an address in a different /30.

whyWrong.0: Addresses go on the port channel, not on members.
whyWrong.2: A member address abandons the logical /30 plan.
whyWrong.3: Both ends cannot use the same address.

prompt: You add a third routed member at each end. Which two checks keep the Layer 3 design? (Choose two.)
options: The new members use no switchport and have no individual IP addresses.
Each new physical member receives the existing Po1 address.
Both new cables terminate on the same intended aggregation partner.
The new members become access ports in VLAN 1.
Both Po1 addresses are removed so the member can inherit them.
explanation: Each new member must be a routed port with no IP address and connect to the same partner. The port channel keeps the link address.

whyWrong.1: The address stays on the port channel.
whyWrong.3: An access port is Layer 2, not routed.
whyWrong.4: The port channel needs its address.

prompt: Both ends show healthy LACP, but they use different hash inputs for outbound traffic. What is the conclusion?
options: The hash methods must match before any member can join.
One endpoint must be using static aggregation despite the LACP records.
The passive endpoint must copy the active endpoint's hash result for each packet.
Different outbound selections are permitted; inspect distribution if it fails service requirements.
explanation: Each end picks its own outbound member with its own hash. Hash methods do not have to match for a bundle to form.

whyWrong.0: Matching hash methods is not a formation requirement.
whyWrong.1: A different hash does not mean a different protocol.
whyWrong.2: LACP roles do not share per-packet hash results.

exhibit.title: Supplied partner and inventory records
exhibit.text:
SW1 Gi0/1 learned partner system 0011.1111.1111, port Gi0/1
SW1 Gi0/2 learned partner system 0022.2222.2222, port Gi0/1
Verified inventory: first system is SW2; second is SW3
SW2 and SW3 are independent switches, not a supported common logical system
Both local ports configured as intended group 1 members

prompt: The design is one two-link bundle between SW1 and SW2, but the records show a different partner system on one member. What do you do?
options: Compare physical connections with the plan and trace the member that reaches SW3.
Force both SW1 members to static on to hide the partner difference.
Rename both remote port channels to match SW1's group number.
Change the local hash method until the two system IDs match.
explanation: One member reaches a different partner system, which is likely SW3. Trace the cabling and fix the physical design.

whyWrong.1: Static on hides the problem without fixing the cabling.
whyWrong.2: Group numbers do not set the partner's identity.
whyWrong.3: The hash method does not change which device a member reaches.

exhibit.title: Supplied partial rollout evidence
exhibit.text:
SW1 Po1(SU): Gi0/1(P), Gi0/2(D)
SW1 Gi0/2: administratively down; correct retained LACP/trunk settings
Cable inspection: Gi0/2 reaches intended SW2 peer, enabled and configured correctly
Both databases: VLANs 10,20,99 active; endpoint VLAN/IP settings verified
SW1 Po1 allows 10,20,99; SW2 Po1 allows 10,99; both native 99
VLAN 10 traffic passes; VLAN 20 does not

prompt: The goal is two active members and working VLANs 10 and 20. Which two changes fix the separate failures? (Choose two.)
options: Enable SW1 Gi0/2 after confirming its intended peer and retained settings.
Replace LACP with static aggregation at both ends.
Add VLAN 20 to SW2 Po1's existing allowed list and verify its members.
Change both native VLANs to 20.
Rename the far-end group number to 1.
explanation: SW1 Gi0/2 is shut down, so only one member is active. SW2's Po1 trunk also excludes VLAN 20, so fix both.

whyWrong.1: LACP already works, so switching to static fixes neither failure.
whyWrong.3: The native VLAN is not the cause of either failure.
whyWrong.4: A group number fixes neither failure.

prompt: How many active member links can an EtherChannel bundle have?
explanation: A bundle has at most 8 active members.

whyWrong.0: Two is the minimum bundle, not the maximum.
whyWrong.1: Four is below the limit of 8.
whyWrong.3: Sixteen is more than the limit of 8 active members.

prompt: Which EtherChannel negotiation protocol is the IEEE standard?
options: PAgP
LACP
DTP
CDP
explanation: LACP is the standard protocol, specified by IEEE 802.1AX (formerly 802.3ad). PAgP is Cisco's.

whyWrong.3: CDP is a discovery protocol.

prompt: Which PAgP mode pair does not form a bundle?
options: desirable / desirable
desirable / auto
auto / auto
on / on
explanation: desirable initiates and auto only responds. Auto/auto has no initiator, so no bundle forms.

whyWrong.0: Desirable ends initiate and form a bundle.
whyWrong.1: Desirable initiates and auto responds, so it forms.
whyWrong.3: Static on at both ends forms a bundle without negotiation.

prompt: Which channel-group mode forms a bundle with no PAgP or LACP negotiation?
options: active
desirable
on
passive
explanation: on is static aggregation with no negotiation protocol. Both ends need compatible static configuration.

whyWrong.3: Passive responds to LACP.
